die-gedanken-sind-frei.credit: Traditional German folk song, first printed c. 1780 (text: LRCLIB transcription)
en: Thoughts are free,
who can guess them?
They drift past
like shadows in the night.
No one can know them,
no hunter shoot them.
And so it remains:
thoughts are free.
I think what I want
and what makes me happy,
but all of it in silence
and as is proper.
My wish and desire
no one can deny me.
And so it remains:
thoughts are free.
And if they lock me up
in a dark dungeon,
all of that is merely
wasted effort,
for my thoughts
tear the barriers
and walls in two:
thoughts are free.
So I will forever
give up my worries
and never again
torment myself with gloomy whims.
In your heart you can
always laugh and joke
and think as well:
thoughts are free.
Thoughts are free.

gruen-gruen-gruen-sind-alle-meine-kleide.credit: Traditional German children's song (text: LRCLIB transcription)
en: Green, green, green are all my clothes,
green, green, green is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so green,
because my sweetheart is a hunter.
Red, red, red are all my clothes,
red, red, red is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so red,
because my sweetheart is a rider.
Blue, blue, blue are all my clothes,
blue, blue, blue is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so blue,
because my sweetheart is a sailor.
Black, black, black are all my clothes,
black, black, black is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so black,
because my sweetheart is a chimney sweep.
White, white, white are all my clothes,
white, white, white is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so white,
because my sweetheart is a miller.
Colourful, colourful, colourful are all my clothes,
colourful, colourful, colourful is everything I have.
That's why I love everything that's so colourful,
because my sweetheart is a painter.

muss-i-denn.credit: Traditional Swabian folk song, text by Heinrich Wagner (1824), first verse
de: Muss i denn, muss i denn zum Städtele hinaus,
Städtele hinaus, und du, mein Schatz, bleibst hier?
Wenn i komm, wenn i komm, wenn i wiedrum komm,
wiedrum komm, kehr i ein, mein Schatz, bei dir.
Kann i gleich net allweil bei dir sein,
han i doch mei Freud an dir;
wenn i komm, wenn i komm, wenn i wiedrum komm,
wiedrum komm, kehr i ein, mein Schatz, bei dir.
en: Must I then, must I then leave the little town,
leave the little town, while you, my darling, stay here?
When I come, when I come, when I come back again,
come back again, I'll stop by you, my darling.
Even if I can't always be with you,
I still take joy in you;
when I come, when I come, when I come back again,
come back again, I'll stop by you, my darling.

erlkoenig.credit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (†1832), text: Wikisource
en: Who rides so late through night and wind?
It is the father with his child;
he holds the boy close in his arm,
he grips him safely, he keeps him warm.
My son, why do you hide your face so fearfully? —
Father, don't you see the Elf King?
The Elf King with his crown and train? —
My son, it is a strip of mist. —
"You dear child, come, go with me!
I'll play such lovely games with you;
many colourful flowers are on the shore,
my mother has many a golden robe." —
My father, my father, and don't you hear
what the Elf King quietly promises me? —
Be calm, stay calm, my child;
the wind is rustling in dry leaves. —
"Will you, fine boy, come with me?
My daughters shall look after you well;
my daughters lead the nightly round dance
and rock and dance and sing you to sleep." —
My father, my father, and don't you see there
the Elf King's daughters in that gloomy place? —
My son, my son, I see it clearly:
it's the old willows looking so grey. —
"I love you, your beautiful form tempts me;
and if you're not willing, I'll use force." —
My father, my father, now he's grabbing me!
The Elf King has hurt me! —
The father shudders; he rides swiftly,
he holds the groaning child in his arms,
reaches the farm with great effort;
in his arms the child was dead.

gefunden.credit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (†1832), text: Wikisource
en: I walked in the woods
just by myself,
and looking for nothing,
that was my mind.
In the shade I saw
a little flower standing,
shining like stars,
beautiful like little eyes.
I wanted to pick it,
then it said gently:
Shall I be picked
only to wilt?
I dug it up with all
its little roots,
I carried it to the garden
by the pretty house.
And planted it again
in a quiet spot;
now it keeps branching
and blooms on and on.
His gaze, from the passing of the bars,
has grown so tired that it holds nothing more.
To him it seems there are a thousand bars
and behind a thousand bars no world.
The soft walk of supple, strong steps,
that turns in the very smallest circle,
is like a dance of strength around a centre
in which a great will stands stunned.
Only sometimes the curtain of the pupil
silently slides up —. Then an image goes in,
goes through the limbs' tense stillness —
and in the heart stops being.
I don't know what it should mean
that I am so sad;
a fairy tale from olden times
won't leave my mind.
The air is cool and it grows dark,
and calmly flows the Rhine;
the summit of the mountain sparkles
in the evening sunshine.
The most beautiful maiden sits
up there, wondrous,
her golden jewellery flashes,
she combs her golden hair.
She combs it with a golden comb
and sings a song as she does;
it has a wondrous,
mighty melody.
The boatman in his little boat
is seized by it with wild pain;
he does not see the rocky reefs,
he only looks up to the heights.
I believe the waves swallow
boatman and boat in the end;
and that, with her singing,
the Lore-Ley has done.
